# async_fs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-fs/

## Expand description

Async filesystem primitives.

This crate is an async version of [ std::fs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

This crate uses [ blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking) to offload blocking I/O onto a thread pool.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a new file and write some bytes to it:

```
use async_fs::File;
use futures_lite::io::AsyncWriteExt;
let mut file = File::create("a.txt").await?;
file.write_all(b"Hello, world!").await?;
file.flush().await?;
```

- `pub use std::fs::`- [Permissions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.Permissions.html);

# async-fs

Async filesystem primitives.

This crate is an async version of `std::fs`.

## Implementation

This crate uses [ blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking) to offload blocking I/O onto a thread pool.

## Examples

Create a new file and write some bytes to it:

```
use File;
use AsyncWriteExt;
let mut file = create.await?;
file.write_all.await?;
file.flush.await?;
```

# async_lock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-lock/^3.0.0/

## Expand description

Async synchronization primitives.

This crate provides the following primitives:

- `Barrier`
- `Mutex`
- `RwLock`
- `Semaphore`

[§](https://docs.rs#relationship-with-stdsync)Relationship with `std::sync`

In general, you should consider using [ std::sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html) types over types from this crate.

There are two primary use cases for types from this crate:

- You need to use a synchronization primitive in a `no_std`environment.
- You need to hold a lock across an `.await`point. (Holding an`std::sync``.await`will make your future non-`Send`, and is also highly likely to cause deadlocks.)

If you already use `libstd` and you aren’t holding locks across await points (there is a
Clippy lint called [ await_holding_lock](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/stable/index.html#/await_holding_lock) that emits warnings for this scenario), you should
consider

[instead of this crate. Those types are optimized for the currently running operating system, are less complex and are generally much faster.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html)

`std::sync`In contrast, `async-lock`’s notification system uses `std::sync::Mutex` under the hood if
the `std` feature is enabled, and will fall back to a significantly slower strategy if it is
not. So, there are few cases where `async-lock` is a win for performance over [ std::sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [futures](https://docs.rs/futures/index.html)
- Named futures for use with `async_lock`primitives.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Barrier](https://docs.rs/struct.Barrier.html)
- A counter to synchronize multiple tasks at the same time.

# blocking - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/blocking/^1.3.0/

## Expand description

A thread pool for isolating blocking I/O in async programs.

Sometimes there’s no way to avoid blocking I/O. Consider files or stdin, which have weak async
support on modern operating systems. While [IOCP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Input/output_completion_port), [AIO](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/io_submit.2.html), and [io_uring](https://lwn.net/Articles/776703) are possible
solutions, they’re not always available or ideal.

Since blocking is not allowed inside futures, we must move blocking I/O onto a special thread pool provided by this crate. The pool dynamically spawns and stops threads depending on the current number of running I/O jobs.

Note that there is a limit on the number of active threads. Once that limit is hit, a running job has to finish before others get a chance to run. When a thread is idle, it waits for the next job or shuts down after a certain timeout.

The default number of threads (set to 500) can be altered by setting BLOCKING_MAX_THREADS environment variable with value between 1 and 10000.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Read the contents of a file:

```
use blocking::unblock;
use std::fs;
let contents = unblock(|| fs::read_to_string("file.txt")).await?;
println!("{}", contents);
```
Read a file and pipe its contents to stdout:

```
use blocking::{unblock, Unblock};
use futures_lite::io;
use std::fs::File;
let input = unblock(|| File::open("file.txt")).await?;
let input = Unblock::new(input);
let mut output = Unblock::new(std::io::stdout());
io::copy(input, &mut output).await?;
```
Iterate over the contents of a directory:

```
use blocking::Unblock;
use futures_lite::prelude::*;
use std::fs;
let mut dir = Unblock::new(fs::read_dir(".")?);
while let Some(item) = dir.next().await {
    println!("{}", item?.file_name().to_string_lossy());
}
```
Spawn a process:

```
use blocking::unblock;
use std::process::Command;
let out = unblock(|| Command::new("dir").output()).await?;
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use async_task::`- [Task](https://docs.rs/async-task/4.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_task/task/struct.Task.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Unblock](https://docs.rs/struct.Unblock.html)
- Runs blocking I/O on a thread pool.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [unblock](https://docs.rs/fn.unblock.html)
- Runs blocking code on a thread pool.

# futures_lite - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-lite/^2.0.0/

## Expand description

Futures, streams, and async I/O combinators.

This crate is a subset of [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) that compiles an order of magnitude faster, fixes minor
warts in its API, fills in some obvious gaps, and removes almost all unsafe code from it.

In short, this crate aims to be more enjoyable than [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) but still fully compatible with
it.

The API for this crate is intentionally constrained. Please consult the [features list](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite/blob/master/FEATURES.md) for
APIs that are occluded from this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use futures_lite::future;
fn main() {
    future::block_on(async {
        println!("Hello world!");
    })
}
```

# async_fs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-fs/latest/target-redirect/async_fs/

## Expand description

Async filesystem primitives.

This crate is an async version of [ std::fs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

This crate uses [ blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking) to offload blocking I/O onto a thread pool.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a new file and write some bytes to it:

```
use async_fs::File;
use futures_lite::io::AsyncWriteExt;
let mut file = File::create("a.txt").await?;
file.write_all(b"Hello, world!").await?;
file.flush().await?;
```

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# blocking - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/blocking

## Expand description

A thread pool for isolating blocking I/O in async programs.

Sometimes there’s no way to avoid blocking I/O. Consider files or stdin, which have weak async
support on modern operating systems. While [IOCP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Input/output_completion_port), [AIO](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/io_submit.2.html), and [io_uring](https://lwn.net/Articles/776703) are possible
solutions, they’re not always available or ideal.

Since blocking is not allowed inside futures, we must move blocking I/O onto a special thread pool provided by this crate. The pool dynamically spawns and stops threads depending on the current number of running I/O jobs.

Note that there is a limit on the number of active threads. Once that limit is hit, a running job has to finish before others get a chance to run. When a thread is idle, it waits for the next job or shuts down after a certain timeout.

The default number of threads (set to 500) can be altered by setting BLOCKING_MAX_THREADS environment variable with value between 1 and 10000.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Read the contents of a file:

```
use blocking::unblock;
use std::fs;
let contents = unblock(|| fs::read_to_string("file.txt")).await?;
println!("{}", contents);
```
Read a file and pipe its contents to stdout:

```
use blocking::{unblock, Unblock};
use futures_lite::io;
use std::fs::File;
let input = unblock(|| File::open("file.txt")).await?;
let input = Unblock::new(input);
let mut output = Unblock::new(std::io::stdout());
io::copy(input, &mut output).await?;
```
Iterate over the contents of a directory:

```
use blocking::Unblock;
use futures_lite::prelude::*;
use std::fs;
let mut dir = Unblock::new(fs::read_dir(".")?);
while let Some(item) = dir.next().await {
    println!("{}", item?.file_name().to_string_lossy());
}
```
Spawn a process:

```
use blocking::unblock;
use std::process::Command;
let out = unblock(|| Command::new("dir").output()).await?;
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use async_task::`- [Task](https://docs.rs/async-task/4.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_task/task/struct.Task.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Unblock](https://docs.rs/struct.Unblock.html)

# aws_sdk_elementalinference - Rust

## Expand description

This is the AWS Elemental Inference REST API Reference. It provides information on the URL, request contents, and response contents of each AWS Elemental Inference REST operation.

We assume that you have the IAM permissions that you need to use AWS Elemental Inference via the REST API. We also assume that you are familiar with the features and operations of AWS Elemental Inference as described in *AWS Elemental Inference User Guide*.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Examples are available for many services and operations, check out the

[usage examples](https://github.com/awsdocs/aws-doc-sdk-examples/tree/main/rustv1).

The SDK provides one crate per AWS service. You must add [Tokio](https://crates.io/crates/tokio)
as a dependency within your Rust project to execute asynchronous code. To add `aws-sdk-elementalinference` to
your project, add the following to your **Cargo.toml** file:

```
[dependencies]
aws-config = { version = "1.1.7", features = ["behavior-version-latest"] }
aws-sdk-elementalinference = "1.8.0"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
```
Then in code, a client can be created with the following:

```
use aws_sdk_elementalinference as elementalinference;
#[::tokio::main]

    let config = aws_config::load_from_env().await;
    let client = aws_sdk_elementalinference::Client::new(&config);
    // ... make some calls with the client
    Ok(())
}
```
See the [client documentation](https://docs.rs/aws-sdk-elementalinference/latest/aws_sdk_elementalinference/client/struct.Client.html)
for information on what calls can be made, and the inputs and outputs for each of those calls.

in

[.](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)

`config`The [ operation](https://docs.rs/operation/index.html) module has a submodule for every API, and in each submodule
is the input, output, and error type for that API, as well as builders to construct each of those.

There is a top-level [ Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html) type that encompasses all the errors that the
client can return. Any other error type can be converted to this

`Error` type via the
[trait.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`The other modules within this crate are not required for normal usage.

# aws_sdk_cognitoidentityprovider - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aws-sdk-cognitoidentityprovider/1.123.0/aws_sdk_cognitoidentityprovider/

## Expand description

With the Amazon Cognito user pools API, you can configure user pools and authenticate users. To authenticate users from third-party identity providers (IdPs) in this API, you can [link IdP users to native user profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-identity-federation-consolidate-users.html). Learn more about the authentication and authorization of federated users at [Adding user pool sign-in through a third party](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-identity-federation.html) and in the [User pool federation endpoints and managed login reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-userpools-server-contract-reference.html).

This API reference provides detailed information about API operations and object types in Amazon Cognito.

Along with resource management operations, the Amazon Cognito user pools API includes classes of operations and authorization models for client-side and server-side authentication of users. You can interact with operations in the Amazon Cognito user pools API as any of the following subjects.

- An administrator who wants to configure user pools, app clients, users, groups, or other user pool functions.
- A server-side app, like a web application, that wants to use its Amazon Web Services privileges to manage, authenticate, or authorize a user.
- A client-side app, like a mobile app, that wants to make unauthenticated requests to manage, authenticate, or authorize a user.

For more information, see [Understanding API, OIDC, and managed login pages authentication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/authentication-flows-public-server-side.html#user-pools-API-operations) in the *Amazon Cognito Developer Guide*.

With your Amazon Web Services SDK, you can build the logic to support operational flows in every use case for this API. You can also make direct REST API requests to [Amazon Cognito user pools service endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/cognito_identity.html#cognito_identity_your_user_pools_region). The following links can get you started with the CognitoIdentityProvider client in supported Amazon Web Services SDKs.

To get started with an Amazon Web Services SDK, see [Tools to Build on Amazon Web Services](http://aws.amazon.com/developer/tools/). For example actions and scenarios, see [Code examples for Amazon Cognito Identity Provider using Amazon Web Services SDKs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/service_code_examples_cognito-identity-provider.html).

# aws_sdk_config - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aws-sdk-config/1.113.0/aws_sdk_config/

## Expand description

Config provides a way to keep track of the configurations of all the Amazon Web Services resources associated with your Amazon Web Services account. You can use Config to get the current and historical configurations of each Amazon Web Services resource and also to get information about the relationship between the resources. An Amazon Web Services resource can be an Amazon Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, an Elastic Block Store (EBS) volume, an elastic network Interface (ENI), or a security group. For a complete list of resources currently supported by Config, see [Supported Amazon Web Services resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/resource-config-reference.html#supported-resources).

You can access and manage Config through the Amazon Web Services Management Console, the Amazon Web Services Command Line Interface (Amazon Web Services CLI), the Config API, or the Amazon Web Services SDKs for Config. This reference guide contains documentation for the Config API and the Amazon Web Services CLI commands that you can use to manage Config. The Config API uses the Signature Version 4 protocol for signing requests. For more information about how to sign a request with this protocol, see [Signature Version 4 Signing Process](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/signature-version-4.html). For detailed information about Config features and their associated actions or commands, as well as how to work with Amazon Web Services Management Console, see [What Is Config](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/WhatIsConfig.html) in the *Config Developer Guide*.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Examples are available for many services and operations, check out the

[usage examples](https://github.com/awsdocs/aws-doc-sdk-examples/tree/main/rustv1).

The SDK provides one crate per AWS service. You must add [Tokio](https://crates.io/crates/tokio)
as a dependency within your Rust project to execute asynchronous code. To add `aws-sdk-config` to
your project, add the following to your **Cargo.toml** file:

```
[dependencies]
aws-config = { version = "1.1.7", features = ["behavior-version-latest"] }
aws-sdk-config = "1.113.0"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
```
Then in code, a client can be created with the following:

```
use aws_sdk_config as config;
#[::tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), config::Error> {
    let config = aws_config::load_from_env().await;
    let client = aws_sdk_config::Client::new(&config);
    // ... make some calls with the client
    Ok(())
}
```
See the [client documentation](https://docs.rs/aws-sdk-config/latest/aws_sdk_config/client/struct.Client.html)
for information on what calls can be made, and the inputs and outputs for each of those calls.

## What is Yerba?

Yerba is a lossless YAML editing tool. It lets you programmatically read, modify, and enforce formatting in YAML files while preserving their original structure, including comments, blank lines, quote styles, and key ordering.

Most YAML libraries parse a file into a data structure and serialize it back, discarding all formatting in the process. Yerba operates on the concrete syntax tree (CST), so your edits are surgical: only the targeted values change, and everything else stays exactly as it was.

Yerba is available as:

- A **standalone CLI binary**with zero runtime dependencies
- A **Rust crate**for embedding in Rust applications
- A **Ruby gem**for programmatic YAML editing from Ruby

Yerba was born out of the need to manage, validate, and enforce consistent formatting for hundreds of YAML data files in the [RubyEvents.org](https://github.com/rubyevents/rubyevents) project.

## CLI Usage

The `yerba` CLI follows a consistent pattern:

```
yerba <command> <file> <selector> [value] [options]
```
Selectors use dot-notation for nested keys, brackets for array access, and support glob patterns for operating on multiple files at once.

### Selectors

Selectors let you address any node in a YAML document:

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | A single key | `"database.host"` |
| `key.nested` | Nested key path | `"database.settings.pool"` |
| `[]` | All items in array | `"[].title"` |
| `[N]` | Item at index | `"[0].title"` |
| `[].key[].nested` | Nested array access | `"[].speakers[].name"` |

### Conditions

Conditions filter which items a command operates on:

| Syntax | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `.key == value` | Equality | `".kind == keynote"` |
| `.key != value` | Inequality | `".status != draft"` |
| `.key contains val` | Substring or member | `".title contains Ruby"` |
| `.key not_contains val` | Negated contains | `".title not_contains test"` |

**Key styles** (`--keys`):

| Style | Symbol | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `plain` | — | `host: value` |
| `single` | `'` | `'host': value` |
| `double` | `"` | `"host": value` |

**Value styles** (`--values`):

| Style | Symbol | Example | Behavior | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `plain` | — | `host: localhost` | Unquoted | |
| `single` | `'` | `host: 'localhost'` | Single-quoted | |
| `double` | `"` | `host: "localhost"` | Double-quoted, supports `\n`escapes | |
| `literal` | `\ | -` | Preserves newlines | Strip trailing newline |
| `literal-clip` | `\ | ` | Preserves newlines | Keep one trailing newline |
| `literal-keep` | `\ | +` | Preserves newlines | Keep all trailing newlines |
| `folded` | `>-` | Folds newlines to spaces | Strip trailing newline | |
| `folded-clip` | `>` | Folds newlines to spaces | Keep one trailing newline | |
| `folded-keep` | `>+` | Folds newlines to spaces | Keep all trailing newlines |

Block scalars are only converted when scoped to a specific selector. An unscoped `--values double` will not touch existing block scalars.

`Yerbafile`

A `Yerbafile` is a YAML configuration file that defines formatting and editing rules as pipelines of operations that are applied to your files across your project.

Use `yerba init` to create one, then `yerba apply` to apply all rules, or `yerba check` to verify compliance (exits with code `1` if files would change):

```
```
A Yerbafile supports a global `pipeline` that runs on all matching files, plus per-rule pipelines for file-specific steps. Global steps run first, then per-rule steps refine or override:

```
files: "data/**/*.yml"
pipeline:
  - directives:
      max: 1
      ensure: true
  - collection_style:
      style: block
  - sequence_indent:
      style: indented
  - quote_style:
      key_style: plain
      value_style: double
rules:
  - files: "data/**/videos.yml"
    pipeline:
      - quote_style:
          path: "[].speakers"
          value_style: plain
      - sort_keys:
          path: "[]"
          order:
            - id
            - title
            - speakers
  - files: "data/speakers.yml"
    pipeline:
      - sort_keys:
          path: "[]"
          order:
            - name
            - slug
            - github
      - sort:
          by: name
```
Available pipeline steps:

- `quote_style`Enforce quote style on keys and/or values, optionally scoped by path
- `collection_style`Enforce flow or block style on collections
- `sequence_indent`Enforce compact or indented sequence style
- `sort_keys`Reorder keys to match a predefined list
- `sort`Sort sequence items by field(s)
- `blank_lines`Enforce blank lines between sequence entries
- `set`Set a value (supports conditions)
- `insert`Insert a new key or sequence item
- `delete`Remove a key (supports conditions)
- `rename`Rename a key
- `remove`Remove an item from a sequence
- `directives`Add or remove the document start marker (- `---`), with optional- `max`validation
- `unique`Find or remove duplicate items in a sequence
- `schema`Validate against a JSON schema (with optional- `path`for scoping)

This makes it easy to enforce project-wide YAML conventions in CI:

```
```
## Ruby API

Yerba includes a native C extension (backed by the same Rust core) that provides a full Ruby API for YAML editing.

### Parsing

Create a document from a file path or from a string:

```
document = Yerba.parse_file()
document = Yerba.parse()
```
### Creating Documents

Build documents from Ruby objects:

```
document = Yerba::Document.from({ name: , tags: [, ] })
document = Yerba::Document.from([{ id: , title:  }])
```
Build incrementally using `Document.new` and `root=`:

```
document = Yerba::Document.new
document.root = {}
document[] =
document[] =
document[] = [, ]
document[] = { host: , port: 5432 }
document.save_to!()
```
```
---
name: Event 123
kind: conference
tags:
  - ruby
  - rails
config:
  host: localhost
  port: 5432
```
Or start with `Document.from` and keep building:

```
document = Yerba::Document.from({ name:  })
document[] = []
document[] <<
document[] <<
```
Build a sequence document and append entries:

```
document = Yerba::Document.new
document.root = []
document << { id: , title: , speakers: [] }
document << { id: , title: , speakers: [, ] }
document.save_to!()
```
`document["key"]` and `document << item` are shortcuts for `document.root["key"]` and `document.root << item`.

### Reading Values

Use bracket notation (`[]`) to navigate the document. Returns typed node objects (`Scalar`, `Map`, or `Sequence`) that are live references — mutations flow back to the document.

All access methods (`[]`, `fetch`, `dig`, `value_at`) accept full selector strings like `"database.host"`, `"[0].title"`, or `"[].speakers[].name"`. In the examples below we prefer the more idiomatic chained bracket style, but the two forms are equivalent:

```
document[][].value  # => "localhost"
document[].value     # => "localhost" (same thing)
```
The returned object type depends on what's at the path:

```
document[]          # => Yerba::Map
document[][]  # => Yerba::Scalar
document[]              # => Yerba::Sequence
```
Scalars expose their value and quote style:

```
scalar = document[][]
scalar.value        # => "localhost"
scalar.quote_style  # => :double
```
Use `fetch` for strict access, it raises `Yerba::SelectorNotFoundError` with "did you mean?" suggestions if the selector doesn't exist:

```
document.fetch()  # => Yerba::Scalar
document.fetch()   # => raises SelectorNotFoundError: ... Did you mean: database.host?
```
Use `dig` to traverse multiple levels, returning `nil` for missing paths:

```
document.dig(, )     # => Yerba::Scalar
document.dig(, 0, )     # => Yerba::Scalar
document.dig(, )  # => nil
```
Use `value_at` to get the plain Ruby value (String, Integer, Hash, Array, etc.) instead of a node object:

```
document.value_at()  # => "localhost"
document.value_at()  # => 5432
document.value_at()       # => {"host" => "localhost", "port" => 5432}
document.value_at()       # => ["First Talk", "Second Talk"]
```
Summary of access methods:

| Method | Not found | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `[]` | `nil` | `Scalar`/`Map`/`Sequence`node |
| `fetch` | raises `SelectorNotFoundError` | `Scalar`/`Map`/`Sequence`node |
| `dig` | `nil` | `Scalar`/`Map`/`Sequence`node |
| `value_at` | `nil` | plain Ruby value |

### Mutations

Modify values in place. The original formatting is preserved:

```
document[][].value =
document.set(, 3306)
```
Set all matching nodes at once with `all: true`:

```
document.set(, , all: true)
```
Insert new keys with positional control:

```
document[].insert(, true, after: )
```
Set arrays and hashes as values, they default to block style:

```
document[][] = [, ]
# tags:
#   - ruby
#   - rails
document[][] = { pool: 5, timeout: 30 }
# settings:
#   pool: 5
#   timeout: 30
```
Use `set` with `style: :flow` for inline formatting:

```
document.root.set(, [, ], style: :flow)
# tags: [ruby, rails]
```
Work with sequences using familiar Ruby patterns:

```
tags = document[]
tags <<
tags << { name: , version:  }
tags.remove()
```
### Sorting

Sort sequences in place. Works on both the document and sequence level:

```
document.sort(by: :name)
document.sort(by: :name, order: :desc)
document.sort(by: :name, order: [, , ])
document.sort()
document.sort(, order: :desc)
document.sort(, order: [, , ])
```
The `by:` option accepts symbols, strings, or dot-prefixed strings (`:name`, `"name"`, `".name"`).

### Querying

Find and filter items in sequences with `find_by`, `where`, and `pluck`:

```
document.find_by(name: )
document.where(role: )
document.pluck(:name)
document.find_by(speakers: { name:  })
document.where(tags: [])
document.find_by(: )
```
These methods work on `Document` (delegates to root), `Sequence`, and `Collection` (searches across files):

```
collection = Yerba.files()
collection.find_by(name: )
collection.where(kind: )
collection.pluck(:name)
```
### Schema Validation

Validate documents against JSON schemas from Ruby:

```
schema = {
  type: ,
  properties: { name: { type:  }, slug: { type:  } },
  required: [, ]
}
document.valid?(schema)                 # => true/false
document.valid?(schema, selector: ) # validate each array item
errors = document.validate(schema, selector: )
errors.each do
  puts
end
```
Also accepts a JSON string:

```
document.valid?()
```
### Quote Style Control

Read and set the quote style on individual scalars:

```
scalar = document[][]
scalar.quote_style # => :double
scalar.quote_style = :single
```
### Collection Style

Read and change how collections are rendered, flow (inline) or block (multi-line):

```
document[].collection_style          # => :block or :flow
document[].collection_style = :flow  # => tags: [ruby, rails]
document[].collection_style = :block # => tags:\n  - ruby\n  - rails
```
Works on both sequences and maps:

```
document[].collection_style = :flow  # => database: {host: localhost, port: 5432}
document[].collection_style = :block # => database:\n  host: localhost\n  port: 5432
```
### Sequence Indent

Control whether sequence items are indented under their key or at the same level:

```
document[].sequence_indent             # => :indented or :compact
document[].sequence_indent = :compact  # compact style
document[].sequence_indent = :indented # indented style
```
```
# :compact               # :indented
tags:                    tags:
- ruby                     - ruby
- rails                    - rails
```
### Location

Get the precise location (line, column, byte offset) of any selector in a document:

```
loc = document[0][].location
loc.start_line    # => 2
loc.start_column  # => 9
loc.end_line      # => 2
loc.end_column    # => 19
loc.start_offset  # => 22
loc.end_offset    # => 32
```
You can also get a location by selector string:

```
document.location()
```
The above is the same as:

```
document[0][].location
document[].location
```
Omit the selector to get the whole document's location:

```
document.location # => #<Yerba::Location start_line=1, ...>
```
Returns `nil` for non-existent selectors. Use `locations` for wildcard selectors that match multiple nodes:

```
locs = document.locations()
locs.each {  puts  }
# line 2
# line 4
document.locations()
document.locations()
```
### Wildcard Access

When `[]` receives a wildcard selector (containing `[]`), it returns an array of nodes instead of a single node:

```
document[]       # => [Yerba::Scalar, Yerba::Scalar, ...]
document[]  # => [Yerba::Scalar, Yerba::Scalar, ...]
document[]   # => [Yerba::Scalar, Yerba::Scalar, ...]
document[].each {  puts scalar.value }
document[].each {  scalar.value =  }
```
### Collections

Operate on multiple files matching a glob pattern:

```
collection = Yerba.files()
collection.each do
  puts document[0][].value
end
collection.find_by(name: )
collection.where(kind: )
collection.pluck(:name)
collection.apply! do
  document.set(, )
end
```
Use `Collection.get` to retrieve nodes across all matching files in parallel. Returns `Scalar`, `Map`, or `Sequence` objects with `file_path`, `line`, and `selector`:

```
speakers = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
speakers.each do
  puts
end
maps = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
maps.first.class
# => Yerba::Map
sequences = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
sequences.first.class
# => Yerba::Sequence
```
Nodes returned by `Collection.get` lazily load their `Document` on first mutation, so reads are fast and writes work transparently:

```
scalars = Yerba::Collection.get(, )
scalars.first.value =
scalars.first.document.save!
```
### Saving

Write changes back to the original file:

```
document.save!
```
Save to a new path:

```
document.save_to!()
```
Or render the document as a string without writing to disk:

```
document.to_s
```

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

# wipe_daemon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wipe-daemon/0.1.0/wipe_daemon/

## Expand description

The wipe local daemon: an `axum` server that exposes the board over HTTP/WS
and serves the embedded human UI. Started by `wipe serve`.

Collaboration remains git-only; this daemon is a *local* convenience for the
human UX. It records each served project in a machine-wide registry so the UI
can list every board you have opened.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AppState](https://docs.rs/struct.AppState.html)
- Shared server state.
- [Project](https://docs.rs/struct.ProjectEntry.html)- Entry
- One registered project.
- [Serve](https://docs.rs/struct.ServeConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration for a `wipe serve`invocation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_projects.html)- projects
- List all registered projects that still have a `.wipe`board, annotating each with its current board name.
- [serve](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html)
- Start the daemon and serve until the process is stopped (Ctrl-C).

# async-fs 2.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-fs/2.2.0

# async-fs

Async filesystem primitives.

This crate is an async version of `std::fs`.

## Implementation

This crate uses [ blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking) to offload blocking I/O onto a thread pool.

## Examples

Create a new file and write some bytes to it:

```
use File;
use AsyncWriteExt;
let mut file = create.await?;
file.write_all.await?;
file.flush.await?;
```

## Expand description

Async filesystem primitives.

This crate is an async version of [ std::fs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

This crate uses [ blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking) to offload blocking I/O onto a thread pool.

```
use async_fs::File;

[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// Copies a file to a new location.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// On success, the total number of bytes copied is returned and equals the length of the `dst`
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// file after this operation.
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// The old contents of `dst` will be overwritten. If `src` and `dst` both point to the same
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// file, then the file will likely get truncated as a result of this operation.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)///
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// If you're working with open [`File`]s and want to copy contents through those types, use
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// [`futures_lite::io::copy()`] instead.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)///
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// # Errors

[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// An error will be returned in the following situations:
[99](https://docs.rs#99)///

[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// * The current process lacks permissions to read `src` or write `dst`.

[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// A stream of entries in a directory.

[316](https://docs.rs#316)pub struct ReadDir(State);
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)/// The state of an asynchronous `ReadDir`.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)/// The `ReadDir` can be either idle or busy performing an asynchronous operation.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)#[allow(clippy::large_enum_variant)] // TODO: Windows-specific
[322](https://docs.rs#322)enum State {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    Idle(Option<std::fs::ReadDir>),
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    Busy(blocking::Task<(std::fs::ReadDir, Option<io::Result<std::fs::DirEntry>>)>),
[325](https://docs.rs#325)}
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)impl fmt::Debug for ReadDir {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        f.debug_struct("ReadDir").finish()
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)}
[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)impl Stream for ReadDir {
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    type Item = io::Result<DirEntry>;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    fn poll_next(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>> {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)        loop {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            match &mut self.0 {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                State::Idle(opt) => {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                    let mut inner = opt.take().unwrap();
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                    // Start the operation asynchronously.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                    self.0 = State::Busy(unblock(move || {
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                        let next = inner.next();
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                        (inner, next)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)                    }));
[347](https://docs.rs#347)                }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)                // Poll the asynchronous operation the file is currently blocked on.
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                State::Busy(task) => {
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                    let (inner, opt) = ready!(task.poll(cx));
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                    self.0 = State::Idle(Some(inner));
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                    return Poll::Ready(opt.map(|res| res.map(|inner| DirEntry(Arc::new(inner)))));
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            }
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        }
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    }
[357](https://docs.rs#357)}

[714](https://docs.rs#714)/// A builder for creating directories with configurable options.
[715](https://docs.rs#715)///
[716](https://docs.rs#716)/// For Unix-specific options, import the [`DirBuilderExt`][`std::os::unix::fs::DirBuilderExt`]
[717](https://docs.rs#717)/// trait.
[718](https://docs.rs#718)#[derive(Debug, Default)]
[719](https://docs.rs#719)pub struct DirBuilder {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)    /// Set to `true` if non-existent parent directories should be created.
[721](https://docs.rs#721)    recursive: bool,
[722](https://docs.rs#722)
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    /// Unix mode for newly created directories.
[724](https://docs.rs#724)    #[cfg(unix)]
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    mode: Option<u32>,
[726](https://docs.rs#726)}
[727](https://docs.rs#727)
[728](https://docs.rs#728)impl DirBuilder {
[729](https://docs.rs#729)    /// Creates a blank set of options.
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    ///
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    /// The [`recursive()`][`DirBuilder::recursive()`] option is initially set to `false`.
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    ///
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    /// # Examples
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    ///
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// ```
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    /// use async_fs::DirBuilder;
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    ///
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    /// let builder = DirBuilder::new();
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// ```
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    pub fn new() -> DirBuilder {
[741](https://docs.rs#741)        #[cfg(not(unix))]
[742](https://docs.rs#742)        let builder = DirBuilder { recursive: false };
[743](https://docs.rs#743)
[744](https://docs.rs#744)        #[cfg(unix)]
[745](https://docs.rs#745)        let builder = DirBuilder {
[746](https://docs.rs#746)            recursive: false,
[747](https://docs.rs#747)            mode: None,
[748](https://docs.rs#748)        };
[749](https://docs.rs#749)
[750](https://docs.rs#750)        builder
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    }
[752](https://docs.rs#752)
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// Sets the option for recursive mode.
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    ///
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    /// When set to `true`, this option means all parent directories should be created recursively
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    /// if they don't exist. Parents are created with the same permissions as the final directory.
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    ///
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    /// This option is initially set to `false`.
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    ///
[760](https://docs.rs#760)    /// # Examples
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    ///
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    /// ```
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    /// use async_fs::DirBuilder;
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    ///
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    /// let mut builder = DirBuilder::new();
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    /// builder.recursive(true);
[767](https://docs.rs#767)    /// ```
[768](https://docs.rs#768)    pub fn recursive(&mut self, recursive: bool) -> &mut Self {
[769](https://docs.rs#769)        self.recursive = recursive;
[770](https://docs.rs#770)        self
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    }
[772](https://docs.rs#772)
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    /// Creates a directory with the configured options.
[774](https://docs.rs#774)    ///
[775](https://docs.rs#775)    /// It is considered an error if the directory already exists unless recursive mode is enabled.
[776](https://docs.rs#776)    ///
[777](https://docs.rs#777)    /// # Errors
[778](https://docs.rs#778)    ///
[779](https://docs.rs#779)    /// An error will be returned in the following situations:
[780](https://docs.rs#780)    ///
[781](https://docs.rs#781)    /// * `path` already points to an existing file or directory.
[782](https://docs.rs#782)    /// * The current process lacks permissions to create the directory or its missing parents.
[783](https://docs.rs#783)    /// * Some other I/O error occurred.
[784](https://docs.rs#784)    ///
[785](https://docs.rs#785)    /// # Examples
[786](https://docs.rs#786)    ///
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    /// ```no_run
[788](https://docs.rs#788)    /// use async_fs::DirBuilder;
[789](https://docs.rs#789)    ///
[790](https://docs.rs#790)    /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    /// DirBuilder::new()
[792](https://docs.rs#792)    ///     .recursive(true)
[793](https://docs.rs#793)    ///     .create("./some/directory")
[794](https://docs.rs#794)    ///     .await?;
[795](https://docs.rs#795)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    /// ```
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    pub fn create<P: AsRef<Path>>(&self, path: P) -> impl Future<Output = io::Result<()>> {
[798](https://docs.rs#798)        let mut builder = std::fs::DirBuilder::new();
[799](https://docs.rs#799)        builder.recursive(self.recursive);
[800](https://docs.rs#800)
[801](https://docs.rs#801)        #[cfg(unix)]
[802](https://docs.rs#802)        {
[803](https://docs.rs#803)            if let Some(mode) = self.mode {
[804](https://docs.rs#804)                std::os::unix::fs::DirBuilderExt::mode(&mut builder, mode);
[805](https://docs.rs#805)            }
[806](https://docs.rs#806)        }
[807](https://docs.rs#807)
[808](https://docs.rs#808)        let path = path.as_ref().to_owned();
[809](https://docs.rs#809)        unblock(move || builder.create(path))
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    }
[811](https://docs.rs#811)}
[812](https://docs.rs#812)
[813](https://docs.rs#813)#[cfg(unix)]
[814](https://docs.rs#814)impl unix::DirBuilderExt for DirBuilder {
[815](https://docs.rs#815)    fn mode(&mut self, mode: u32) -> &mut Self {
[816](https://docs.rs#816)        self.mode = Some(mode);
[817](https://docs.rs#817)        self
[818](https://docs.rs#818)    }

[820](https://docs.rs#820)
[821](https://docs.rs#821)/// An open file on the filesystem.
[822](https://docs.rs#822)///
[823](https://docs.rs#823)/// Depending on what options the file was opened with, this type can be used for reading and/or
[824](https://docs.rs#824)/// writing.
[825](https://docs.rs#825)///
[826](https://docs.rs#826)/// Files are automatically closed when they get dropped and any errors detected on closing are
[827](https://docs.rs#827)/// ignored. Use the [`sync_all()`][`File::sync_all()`] method before dropping a file if such
[828](https://docs.rs#828)/// errors need to be handled.
[829](https://docs.rs#829)///
[830](https://docs.rs#830)/// **NOTE:** If writing to a file, make sure to call
[831](https://docs.rs#831)/// [`flush()`][`futures_lite::io::AsyncWriteExt::flush()`], [`sync_data()`][`File::sync_data()`],
[832](https://docs.rs#832)/// or [`sync_all()`][`File::sync_all()`] before dropping the file or else some written data
[833](https://docs.rs#833)/// might get lost!
[834](https://docs.rs#834)///
[835](https://docs.rs#835)/// # Examples
[836](https://docs.rs#836)///
[837](https://docs.rs#837)/// Create a new file and write some bytes to it:
[838](https://docs.rs#838)///
[839](https://docs.rs#839)/// ```no_run
[840](https://docs.rs#840)/// use async_fs::File;
[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// use futures_lite::io::AsyncWriteExt;
[842](https://docs.rs#842)///
[843](https://docs.rs#843)/// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)/// let mut file = File::create("a.txt").await?;
[845](https://docs.rs#845)///
[846](https://docs.rs#846)/// file.write_all(b"Hello, world!").await?;
[847](https://docs.rs#847)/// file.flush().await?;
[848](https://docs.rs#848)/// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[849](https://docs.rs#849)/// ```
[850](https://docs.rs#850)///
[851](https://docs.rs#851)/// Read the contents of a file into a vector of bytes:
[852](https://docs.rs#852)///
[853](https://docs.rs#853)/// ```no_run
[854](https://docs.rs#854)/// use async_fs::File;
[855](https://docs.rs#855)/// use futures_lite::io::AsyncReadExt;
[856](https://docs.rs#856)///
[857](https://docs.rs#857)/// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[858](https://docs.rs#858)/// let mut file = File::open("a.txt").await?;
[859](https://docs.rs#859)///
[860](https://docs.rs#860)/// let mut contents = Vec::new();
[861](https://docs.rs#861)/// file.read_to_end(&mut contents).await?;
[862](https://docs.rs#862)/// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[863](https://docs.rs#863)/// ```
[864](https://docs.rs#864)pub struct File {
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    /// Always accessible reference to the file.
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    file: Arc<std::fs::File>,
[867](https://docs.rs#867)
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    /// Performs blocking I/O operations on a thread pool.
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    unblock: Mutex<Unblock<ArcFile>>,
[870](https://docs.rs#870)
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    /// Logical file cursor, tracked when reading from the file.
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    ///
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    /// This will be set to an error if the file is not seekable.
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    read_pos: Option<io::Result<u64>>,
[875](https://docs.rs#875)
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    /// Set to `true` if the file needs flushing.

[878](https://docs.rs#878)}

[880](https://docs.rs#880)impl File {

[891](https://docs.rs#891)        }

[915](https://docs.rs#915)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[916](https://docs.rs#916)    /// ```

[954](https://docs.rs#954)    /// Synchronizes OS-internal buffered contents and metadata to disk.
[955](https://docs.rs#955)    ///
[956](https://docs.rs#956)    /// This function will ensure that all in-memory data reaches the filesystem.
[957](https://docs.rs#957)    ///
[958](https://docs.rs#958)    /// This can be used to handle errors that would otherwise only be caught by closing the file.
[959](https://docs.rs#959)    /// When a file is dropped, errors in synchronizing this in-memory data are ignored.
[960](https://docs.rs#960)    ///
[961](https://docs.rs#961)    /// # Examples
[962](https://docs.rs#962)    ///
[963](https://docs.rs#963)    /// ```no_run
[964](https://docs.rs#964)    /// use async_fs::File;
[965](https://docs.rs#965)    /// use futures_lite::io::AsyncWriteExt;
[966](https://docs.rs#966)    ///
[967](https://docs.rs#967)    /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[968](https://docs.rs#968)    /// let mut file = File::create("a.txt").await?;
[969](https://docs.rs#969)    ///
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    /// file.write_all(b"Hello, world!").await?;
[971](https://docs.rs#971)    /// file.sync_all().await?;
[972](https://docs.rs#972)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    /// ```
[974](https://docs.rs#974)    pub async fn sync_all(&self) -> io::Result<()> {
[975](https://docs.rs#975)        let mut inner = self.unblock.lock().await;
[976](https://docs.rs#976)        inner.flush().await?;
[977](https://docs.rs#977)        let file = self.file.clone();
[978](https://docs.rs#978)        unblock(move || file.sync_all()).await
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    }
[980](https://docs.rs#980)
[981](https://docs.rs#981)    /// Synchronizes OS-internal buffered contents to disk.
[982](https://docs.rs#982)    ///
[983](https://docs.rs#983)    /// This is similar to [`sync_all()`][`File::sync_data()`], except that file metadata may not
[984](https://docs.rs#984)    /// be synchronized.
[985](https://docs.rs#985)    ///
[986](https://docs.rs#986)    /// This is intended for use cases that must synchronize the contents of the file, but don't
[987](https://docs.rs#987)    /// need the file metadata synchronized to disk.
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    ///
[989](https://docs.rs#989)    /// Note that some platforms may simply implement this in terms of
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    /// [`sync_all()`][`File::sync_data()`].
[991](https://docs.rs#991)    ///
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    /// # Examples
[993](https://docs.rs#993)    ///
[994](https://docs.rs#994)    /// ```no_run
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    /// use async_fs::File;
[996](https://docs.rs#996)    /// use futures_lite::io::AsyncWriteExt;
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    ///
[998](https://docs.rs#998)    /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    /// let mut file = File::create("a.txt").await?;
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    ///
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    /// file.write_all(b"Hello, world!").await?;
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    /// file.sync_data().await?;
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    /// ```
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    pub async fn sync_data(&self) -> io::Result<()> {
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)        let mut inner = self.unblock.lock().await;
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)        inner.flush().await?;
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)        let file = self.file.clone();
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)        unblock(move || file.sync_data()).await
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)    }

[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)    /// Truncates or extends the file.
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)    ///
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)    /// If `size` is less than the current file size, then the file will be truncated. If it is
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)    /// greater than the current file size, then the file will be extended to `size` and have all
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)    /// intermediate data filled with zeros.
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)    ///

[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)    /// file.set_len(10).await?;
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    /// ```
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)    pub async fn set_len(&self, size: u64) -> io::Result<()> {
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)        let mut inner = self.unblock.lock().await;

[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)        let file = self.file.clone();
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)        unblock(move || file.set_len(size)).await
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)    }

[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)    /// Repositions the cursor after reading.
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)    ///
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)    /// When reading from a file, actual file reads run asynchronously in the background, which
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)    /// means the real file cursor is usually ahead of the logical cursor, and the data between
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)    /// them is buffered in memory. This kind of buffering is an important optimization.
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)    ///
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)    /// After reading ends, if we decide to perform a write or a seek operation, the real file
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)    /// cursor must first be repositioned back to the correct logical position.
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)    fn poll_reposition(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<io::Result<()>> {
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)        if let Some(Ok(read_pos)) = self.read_pos {
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)            ready!(Pin::new(self.unblock.get_mut()).poll_seek(cx, SeekFrom::Start(read_pos)))?;
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)        }
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)        self.read_pos = None;
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)        Poll::Ready(Ok(()))
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)    }

[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)impl AsyncRead for File {
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)    fn poll_read(
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)        mut self: Pin<&mut Self>,
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)        cx: &mut Context<'_>,
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)        buf: &mut [u8],
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)    ) -> Poll<io::Result<usize>> {
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)        // Before reading begins, remember the current cursor position.
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)        if self.read_pos.is_none() {
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)            // Initialize the logical cursor to the current position in the file.
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)            self.read_pos = Some(ready!(self.as_mut().poll_seek(cx, SeekFrom::Current(0))));
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)        }
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)        let n = ready!(Pin::new(self.unblock.get_mut()).poll_read(cx, buf))?;
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)        // Update the logical cursor if the file is seekable.
[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)        if let Some(Ok(pos)) = self.read_pos.as_mut() {
[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)            *pos += n as u64;
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)        }
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)
[1172](https://docs.rs#1172)        Poll::Ready(Ok(n))
[1173](https://docs.rs#1173)    }
[1174](https://docs.rs#1174)}
[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)impl AsyncWrite for File {
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)    fn poll_write(
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)        mut self: Pin<&mut Self>,
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)        cx: &mut Context<'_>,
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)        buf: &[u8],
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)    ) -> Poll<io::Result<usize>> {
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)        ready!(self.poll_reposition(cx))?;
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)        self.is_dirty = true;
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)        Pin::new(self.unblock.get_mut()).poll_write(cx, buf)
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)    }
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)    fn poll_flush(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<io::Result<()>> {
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)        if self.is_dirty {
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)            ready!(Pin::new(self.unblock.get_mut()).poll_flush(cx))?;
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)            self.is_dirty = false;
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)        }
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)        Poll::Ready(Ok(()))
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)    }
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)    fn poll_close(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<io::Result<()>> {
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)        Pin::new(self.unblock.get_mut()).poll_close(cx)
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)    }

[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)/// A builder for opening files with configurable options.
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)///
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)/// Files can be opened in [`read`][`OpenOptions::read()`] and/or
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)/// [`write`][`OpenOptions::write()`] mode.
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)///
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)/// The [`append`][`OpenOptions::append()`] option opens files in a special writing mode that
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)/// moves the file cursor to the end of file before every write operation.
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)///
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)/// It is also possible to [`truncate`][`OpenOptions::truncate()`] the file right after opening,
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)/// to [`create`][`OpenOptions::create()`] a file if it doesn't exist yet, or to always create a
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)/// new file with [`create_new`][`OpenOptions::create_new()`].
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)///
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)/// # Examples
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)///
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)/// Open a file for reading:
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)///
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)/// ```no_run
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)/// use async_fs::OpenOptions;
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)///
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)/// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)/// let file = OpenOptions::new()
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)///     .read(true)
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)///     .open("a.txt")
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)///     .await?;
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)/// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)/// ```
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)///
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)/// Open a file for both reading and writing, and create it if it doesn't exist yet:
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)///
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)/// ```no_run
[1266](https://docs.rs#1266)/// use async_fs::OpenOptions;
[1267](https://docs.rs#1267)///
[1268](https://docs.rs#1268)/// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[1269](https://docs.rs#1269)/// let file = OpenOptions::new()
[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)///     .read(true)
[1271](https://docs.rs#1271)///     .write(true)
[1272](https://docs.rs#1272)///     .create(true)
[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)///     .open("a.txt")
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)///     .await?;
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)/// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1276](https://docs.rs#1276)/// ```
[1277](https://docs.rs#1277)#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
[1278](https://docs.rs#1278)pub struct OpenOptions(std::fs::OpenOptions);
[1279](https://docs.rs#1279)
[1280](https://docs.rs#1280)impl OpenOptions {
[1281](https://docs.rs#1281)    /// Creates a blank set of options.
[1282](https://docs.rs#1282)    ///
[1283](https://docs.rs#1283)    /// All options are initially set to `false`.
[1284](https://docs.rs#1284)    ///
[1285](https://docs.rs#1285)    /// # Examples
[1286](https://docs.rs#1286)    ///
[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)    /// ```no_run
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)    /// use async_fs::OpenOptions;
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)    ///
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)    /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)    /// let file = OpenOptions::new()
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)    ///     .read(true)
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)    ///     .open("a.txt")
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)    ///     .await?;
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });

[1444](https://docs.rs#1444)    /// Opens a file with the configured options.
[1445](https://docs.rs#1445)    ///
[1446](https://docs.rs#1446)    /// # Errors
[1447](https://docs.rs#1447)    ///
[1448](https://docs.rs#1448)    /// An error will be returned in the following situations:
[1449](https://docs.rs#1449)    ///
[1450](https://docs.rs#1450)    /// * The file does not exist and neither [`create`] nor [`create_new`] were set.
[1451](https://docs.rs#1451)    /// * The file's parent directory does not exist.
[1452](https://docs.rs#1452)    /// * The current process lacks permissions to open the file in the configured mode.
[1453](https://docs.rs#1453)    /// * The file already exists and [`create_new`] was set.
[1454](https://docs.rs#1454)    /// * Invalid combination of options was used, like [`truncate`] was set but [`write`] wasn't,
[1455](https://docs.rs#1455)    ///   or none of [`read`], [`write`], and [`append`] modes was set.
[1456](https://docs.rs#1456)    /// * An OS-level occurred, like too many files are open or the file name is too long.
[1457](https://docs.rs#1457)    /// * Some other I/O error occurred.
[1458](https://docs.rs#1458)    ///
[1459](https://docs.rs#1459)    /// [`read`]: `OpenOptions::read()`
[1460](https://docs.rs#1460)    /// [`write`]: `OpenOptions::write()`
[1461](https://docs.rs#1461)    /// [`append`]: `OpenOptions::append()`
[1462](https://docs.rs#1462)    /// [`truncate`]: `OpenOptions::truncate()`
[1463](https://docs.rs#1463)    /// [`create`]: `OpenOptions::create()`
[1464](https://docs.rs#1464)    /// [`create_new`]: `OpenOptions::create_new()`
[1465](https://docs.rs#1465)    ///
[1466](https://docs.rs#1466)    /// # Examples
[1467](https://docs.rs#1467)    ///
[1468](https://docs.rs#1468)    /// ```no_run
[1469](https://docs.rs#1469)    /// use async_fs::OpenOptions;
[1470](https://docs.rs#1470)    ///
[1471](https://docs.rs#1471)    /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[1472](https://docs.rs#1472)    /// let file = OpenOptions::new()
[1473](https://docs.rs#1473)    ///     .read(true)
[1474](https://docs.rs#1474)    ///     .open("a.txt")
[1475](https://docs.rs#1475)    ///     .await?;
[1476](https://docs.rs#1476)    /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1477](https://docs.rs#1477)    /// ```
[1478](https://docs.rs#1478)    pub fn open<P: AsRef<Path>>(&self, path: P) -> impl Future<Output = io::Result<File>> {
[1479](https://docs.rs#1479)        let path = path.as_ref().to_owned();
[1480](https://docs.rs#1480)        let options = self.0.clone();
[1481](https://docs.rs#1481)        async move {
[1482](https://docs.rs#1482)            let file = unblock(move || options.open(path)).await?;
[1483](https://docs.rs#1483)            Ok(File::new(file, false))
[1484](https://docs.rs#1484)        }
[1485](https://docs.rs#1485)    }

[1609](https://docs.rs#1609)    /// Unix-specific extensions to [`OpenOptions`].
[1610](https://docs.rs#1610)    pub trait OpenOptionsExt: Sealed {
[1611](https://docs.rs#1611)        /// Sets the mode bits that a new file will be created with.
[1612](https://docs.rs#1612)        ///
[1613](https://docs.rs#1613)        /// If a new file is created as part of an [`OpenOptions::open()`] call then this
[1614](https://docs.rs#1614)        /// specified `mode` will be used as the permission bits for the new file.
[1615](https://docs.rs#1615)        ///
[1616](https://docs.rs#1616)        /// If no `mode` is set, the default of `0o666` will be used.
[1617](https://docs.rs#1617)        /// The operating system masks out bits with the system's `umask`, to produce
[1618](https://docs.rs#1618)        /// the final permissions.
[1619](https://docs.rs#1619)        ///
[1620](https://docs.rs#1620)        /// # Examples
[1621](https://docs.rs#1621)        ///
[1622](https://docs.rs#1622)        /// ```no_run
[1623](https://docs.rs#1623)        /// use async_fs::{OpenOptions, unix::OpenOptionsExt};
[1624](https://docs.rs#1624)        ///
[1625](https://docs.rs#1625)        /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[1626](https://docs.rs#1626)        /// let mut options = OpenOptions::new();
[1627](https://docs.rs#1627)        /// // Read/write permissions for owner and read permissions for others.
[1628](https://docs.rs#1628)        /// options.mode(0o644);
[1629](https://docs.rs#1629)        /// let file = options.open("foo.txt").await?;
[1630](https://docs.rs#1630)        /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1631](https://docs.rs#1631)        /// ```
[1632](https://docs.rs#1632)        fn mode(&mut self, mode: u32) -> &mut Self;
[1633](https://docs.rs#1633)
[1634](https://docs.rs#1634)        /// Passes custom flags to the `flags` argument of `open`.
[1635](https://docs.rs#1635)        ///
[1636](https://docs.rs#1636)        /// The bits that define the access mode are masked out with `O_ACCMODE`, to
[1637](https://docs.rs#1637)        /// ensure they do not interfere with the access mode set by Rust's options.
[1638](https://docs.rs#1638)        ///
[1639](https://docs.rs#1639)        /// Custom flags can only set flags, not remove flags set by Rust's options.
[1640](https://docs.rs#1640)        /// This options overwrites any previously set custom flags.
[1641](https://docs.rs#1641)        ///
[1642](https://docs.rs#1642)        /// # Examples
[1643](https://docs.rs#1643)        ///

[1816](https://docs.rs#1816)        /// Sets the `dwSecurityQosFlags` argument to the call to [`CreateFile2`] to
[1817](https://docs.rs#1817)        /// the specified value (or combines it with `custom_flags` and `attributes`
[1818](https://docs.rs#1818)        /// to set the `dwFlagsAndAttributes` for [`CreateFile`]).
[1819](https://docs.rs#1819)        ///
[1820](https://docs.rs#1820)        /// By default `security_qos_flags` is not set. It should be specified when
[1821](https://docs.rs#1821)        /// opening a named pipe, to control to which degree a server process can
[1822](https://docs.rs#1822)        /// act on behalf of a client process (security impersonation level).
[1823](https://docs.rs#1823)        ///
[1824](https://docs.rs#1824)        /// When `security_qos_flags` is not set, a malicious program can gain the
[1825](https://docs.rs#1825)        /// elevated privileges of a privileged Rust process when it allows opening
[1826](https://docs.rs#1826)        /// user-specified paths, by tricking it into opening a named pipe. So
[1827](https://docs.rs#1827)        /// arguably `security_qos_flags` should also be set when opening arbitrary
[1828](https://docs.rs#1828)        /// paths. However the bits can then conflict with other flags, specifically
[1829](https://docs.rs#1829)        /// `FILE_FLAG_OPEN_NO_RECALL`.
[1830](https://docs.rs#1830)        ///
[1831](https://docs.rs#1831)        /// For information about possible values, see [Impersonation Levels] on the
[1832](https://docs.rs#1832)        /// Windows Dev Center site. The `SECURITY_SQOS_PRESENT` flag is set
[1833](https://docs.rs#1833)        /// automatically when using this method.
[1834](https://docs.rs#1834)        ///
[1835](https://docs.rs#1835)        /// # Examples
[1836](https://docs.rs#1836)        ///
[1837](https://docs.rs#1837)        /// ```no_run
[1838](https://docs.rs#1838)        /// use async_fs::{OpenOptions, windows::OpenOptionsExt};
[1839](https://docs.rs#1839)        ///
[1840](https://docs.rs#1840)        /// # futures_lite::future::block_on(async {
[1841](https://docs.rs#1841)        /// let file = OpenOptions::new()
[1842](https://docs.rs#1842)        ///     .write(true)
[1843](https://docs.rs#1843)        ///     .create(true)
[1844](https://docs.rs#1844)        ///     .security_qos_flags(windows_sys::Win32::Storage::FileSystem::SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION)
[1845](https://docs.rs#1845)        ///     .open(r"\\.\pipe\MyPipe")
[1846](https://docs.rs#1846)        ///     .await?;
[1847](https://docs.rs#1847)        /// # std::io::Result::Ok(()) });
[1848](https://docs.rs#1848)        /// ```
[1849](https://docs.rs#1849)        ///
